<reason>Side A built a stronger path to victory by rigorously attacking the proposition's economic and mechanical consequences. A effectively leveraged the opportunity cost of finite stadium capacity—each seat given to a local displaces a tourist who would pay hotel occupancy taxes and inject outside capital, while locals merely recirculate existing money. A also landed decisive pressure on this fiscal point (Q1 in [A3.1]) that B failed to squarely answer, deflecting to year-round tax contributions rather than addressing the marginal revenue loss during the event. A's arbitrage argument (local discounts create resale windfalls unless non-transferable, which causes gridlock) and the supply-and-demand point (removing inventory forces dynamic algorithms to surge remaining prices higher) remained largely unneutralized. B offered a compelling fairness framing and the "extraction vs. reciprocity" dichotomy, but the economic case was vulnerable: the claim that local recirculation matches tourist revenue is economically weaker, and B's "sequencing" defense did not adequately address the displacement of tourists at sellout events. B also failed to robustly defend the "members" loophole, allowing A to argue that paywalled memberships would simply be exploited by brokers.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Pressure Questions round ([A3.1]-[A3.2]) and Rebuttal 2 ([A4.1]-[A4.2]) created the decisive clash. A forced B to explain how replacing tourists with locals generates hotel tax revenue to cover municipal costs—a question B evaded by citing year-round property taxes, which do not address event-specific fiscal spikes. A then turned B's own dilemma question (verification impossibility vs. arbitrage) into a fatal policy trap, arguing that organizers face only bad options. This combination exposed that the proposition subsidizes a lucky few at the expense of city finances and market efficiency.</best_rebuttal>
